Given: plate 10 cm \(\times\) 0.5 cm \(\times\) 0.2 cm, \(H = 0.5 \times 10^{4}\) A m\(^{-1}\), induced magnetic moment \(m = 0.5\) A m\(^{2}\). Take \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m A\(^{-1}\).

Step 1 - volume of the plate.
\(V = (10 \times 10^{-2})(0.5 \times 10^{-2})(0.2 \times 10^{-2}) = 1 \times 10^{-6}\) m\(^{3}\).

Step 2 - magnetisation. By Eq. (11.12), magnetisation is magnetic moment per unit volume:
\(M = \dfrac{m}{V} = \dfrac{0.5}{1 \times 10^{-6}} = 5 \times 10^{5}\) A m\(^{-1}\).

Step 3 - magnetic induction. By Eq. (11.15),
\(B = \mu_{0}(H + M) = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times (0.5 \times 10^{4} + 5 \times 10^{5})\)
\(B = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 5.05 \times 10^{5} = 0.6346\) T.

\(\therefore\) the magnetic induction in the plate is \(B \approx 0.634\) Wb m\(^{-2}\) (T).

Note that the magnetising field \(H\) contributes only 1 % of the bracket here; dropping it would give 0.628 T, so it must be kept.

Given: \(A = 0.25\) cm\(^{2} = 0.25 \times 10^{-4}\) m\(^{2}\), \(H = 4000\) A m\(^{-1}\), \(\phi = 25 \times 10^{-6}\) Wb, \(\mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\) T m A\(^{-1}\).

Step 1 - magnetic induction in the rod.
\(B = \dfrac{\phi}{A} = \dfrac{25 \times 10^{-6}}{0.25 \times 10^{-4}} = 1\) T.

Step 2 - permeability and (a) relative permeability. From \(B = \mu H\) (Eq. 11.18),
\(\mu = \dfrac{B}{H} = \dfrac{1}{4000} = 2.5 \times 10^{-4}\) T m A\(^{-1}\),
\(\mu_{r} = \dfrac{\mu}{\mu_{0}} = \dfrac{2.5 \times 10^{-4}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} = 198.9 \approx 199\)  (a pure number).

Step 3 - (b) magnetic susceptibility. From \(\mu_{r} = 1 + \chi\) (Eq. 11.19),
\(\chi = \mu_{r} - 1 = 197.9 \approx 198\)  (dimensionless).

Step 4 - (c) magnetisation. From \(M = \chi H\) (Eq. 11.17),
\(M = 197.9 \times 4000 = 7.92 \times 10^{5}\) A m\(^{-1}\).

Cross-check by the independent route \(M = \dfrac{B}{\mu_{0}} - H\) (Eq. 11.16) \(= \dfrac{1}{4\pi \times 10^{-7}} - 4000 = 7.92 \times 10^{5}\) A m\(^{-1}\), which agrees.

\(\therefore\) (a) \(\mu_{r} \approx 199\), (b) \(\chi \approx 198\), (c) \(M = 7.92 \times 10^{5}\) A m\(^{-1}\).

The magnet starts in the magnetic meridian, i.e. along the field, so the initial angle is \(\theta = 0\). The magnetic potential energy is \(U = -mB\cos\theta\) (Eq. 11.3), so the work done in rotating the magnet from \(0\) to \(\theta\) is
\(W(\theta) = U(\theta) - U(0) = -mB\cos\theta - (-mB) = mB(1 - \cos\theta)\).

For \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\): \(W_{90} = mB(1 - \cos 90^{\circ}) = mB(1 - 0) = mB\).
For \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\): \(W_{60} = mB(1 - \cos 60^{\circ}) = mB\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right) = \dfrac{mB}{2}\).

Given \(W_{90} = n\,W_{60}\),
\(n = \dfrac{W_{90}}{W_{60}} = \dfrac{mB}{mB/2} = 2\).

\(\therefore n = 2\)  (a pure number; note \(m\) and \(B\) cancel, so the result does not depend on the strength of the magnet or of the field).

Given: \(r = 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\) m, \(v = 2 \times 10^{6}\) m s\(^{-1}\), \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\) C, \(m_{e} = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\) kg.

Orbital magnetic moment. From Eq. (11.10), \(m_{orb} = \dfrac{1}{2}evr\):
\(m_{orb} = \dfrac{1}{2} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 2 \times 10^{6} \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\)
\(m_{orb} = 8.48 \times 10^{-24}\) A m\(^{2}\).

Orbital angular momentum. \(L = m_{e}vr\):
\(L = 9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 2 \times 10^{6} \times 5.3 \times 10^{-11}\)
\(L = 9.646 \times 10^{-35}\) kg m\(^{2}\) s\(^{-1}\) \(= 9.646 \times 10^{-35}\) N m s.

Cross-check with Eq. (11.11): \(\dfrac{m_{orb}}{L} = \dfrac{8.48 \times 10^{-24}}{9.646 \times 10^{-35}} = 8.79 \times 10^{10}\) C kg\(^{-1}\), which is exactly the gyromagnetic ratio \(\dfrac{e}{2m_{e}} = \dfrac{1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{2 \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = 8.79 \times 10^{10}\) C kg\(^{-1}\). The two answers are therefore consistent.

\(\therefore m_{orb} = 8.48 \times 10^{-24}\) A m\(^{2}\) and \(L = 9.65 \times 10^{-35}\) N m s. (Since the electron's charge is negative, \(\vec{m}_{orb}\) points opposite to \(\vec{L}\).)

[Textbook misprint: the stem prints the number density as \( 2.0 \times 10^{26} \) atoms/m. It must be atoms per cubic metre — only then does \( n \, m_{\text{atom}} \) carry the units A m\( ^{-1} \) of a magnetisation, which is what part (a) asks for. The stem is preserved as printed; the answer is unaffected.]

Given: number density \(n = 2.0 \times 10^{26}\) atoms per cubic metre, atomic dipole moment \(m = 1.5 \times 10^{-23}\) A m\(^{2}\), \(T = 27\,^{\circ}\)C \(= 300\) K, \(k_{B} = 1.38 \times 10^{-23}\) J K\(^{-1}\). (The stem prints the number density as 'atoms/m'; it has to be read as atoms per m\(^{3}\), since only then does \(n\,m\) carry the unit A m\(^{-1}\) of a magnetisation.)

(a) Maximum magnetisation intensity. Saturation is the state in which EVERY atomic dipole is aligned with the field, so the moment per unit volume is just the number per unit volume times the moment of each:
\(M_{max} = n\,m = 2.0 \times 10^{26} \times 1.5 \times 10^{-23}\)
\(M_{max} = 3.0 \times 10^{3}\) A m\(^{-1}\).

(b) Can saturation be reached at \(B = 3\) T? Follow the hint and compare the two competing energies.
Thermal energy per atom \(= \dfrac{3}{2}k_{B}T = 1.5 \times 1.38 \times 10^{-23} \times 300 = 6.21 \times 10^{-21}\) J.
Maximum magnetic potential energy of an atom \(= mB = 1.5 \times 10^{-23} \times 3 = 4.5 \times 10^{-23}\) J.
Ratio \(= \dfrac{6.21 \times 10^{-21}}{4.5 \times 10^{-23}} \approx 138\).

The thermal energy available to randomise a dipole is about 138 times the largest energy the field can gain by aligning it, so the random thermal motion overwhelms the aligning torque and only a tiny fraction of the dipoles line up.

\(\therefore\) (a) \(M_{max} = 3.0 \times 10^{3}\) A m\(^{-1}\); (b) NO, saturation magnetisation cannot be achieved at 3 T and 300 K. It would need either a very much stronger field or a very much lower temperature — which is exactly Curie's law \(\chi \propto 1/T\) seen from the other side.

Given: \(m = 2 \times 10^{-2}\) A m\(^{2}\), \(I = 7.2 \times 10^{-7}\) kg m\(^{2}\), 10 complete oscillations in 6 s.

Step 1 - period.
\(T = \dfrac{6}{10} = 0.6\) s.

Step 2 - use the period of angular oscillations of a magnet in a field, Eq. (11.8):
\(T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{I}{mB}}\)  \(\Rightarrow\)  \(T^{2} = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}I}{mB}\)  \(\Rightarrow\)  \(B = \dfrac{4\pi^{2}I}{T^{2}m}\).

Step 3 - substitute.
\(B = \dfrac{4\pi^{2} \times 7.2 \times 10^{-7}}{(0.6)^{2} \times 2 \times 10^{-2}} = \dfrac{2.8424 \times 10^{-5}}{7.2 \times 10^{-3}}\)
\(B = 3.948 \times 10^{-3}\) T.

\(\therefore B = 39.48 \times 10^{-4}\) Wb m\(^{-2}\) (T).

Given: \(B = 700\) gauss \(= 700 \times 10^{-4} = 0.07\) T, \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\), \(\tau = 0.014\) N m.

Part 1 - magnetic moment. From Eq. (11.1), \(\tau = mB\sin\theta\):
\(m = \dfrac{\tau}{B\sin\theta} = \dfrac{0.014}{0.07 \times \sin 30^{\circ}} = \dfrac{0.014}{0.07 \times 0.5} = \dfrac{0.014}{0.035}\)
\(m = 0.4\) A m\(^{2}\).

Part 2 - work done from the most stable to the most unstable position. From Eq. (11.3), \(U = -mB\cos\theta\). The most STABLE position is \(\theta = 0\) (\(\vec{m}\) parallel to \(\vec{B}\), \(U_{min} = -mB\)) and the most UNSTABLE is \(\theta = 180^{\circ}\) (\(\vec{m}\) antiparallel to \(\vec{B}\), \(U_{max} = +mB\)). The work done against the field equals the increase in potential energy:
\(W = U(180^{\circ}) - U(0) = mB - (-mB) = 2mB\)
\(W = 2 \times 0.4 \times 0.07 = 0.056\) J.

\(\therefore m = 0.4\) A m\(^{2}\) and \(W = 0.056\) J.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed key gives \( 9.8 \times 10^{-5} \) T, four times the correct value. Balancing the couple on the suspended needle, the weight at one end exerts a torque \( Mgl \) about the pivot, while the vertical component acts on both poles to give a couple \( q_m B_V (2l) \); equating them gives \( B_V = \dfrac{Mg}{2 q_m} = \dfrac{0.1 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.8}{2 \times 20} = 2.45 \times 10^{-5} \) T, independent of the needle's length. The printed answer keeps the numerator's mantissa \( 9.8 \) and decrements only the exponent, so the division by \( 2 q_m = 40 \) was never carried out. The stem was checked against the page and is faithfully transcribed \( (0.1 \) g, \( 20 \) A m, \( g = 9.8 \) m s\( ^{-2}) \). Independently, \( 9.8 \times 10^{-5} \) T is \( 98 \) \( \mu \)T, which exceeds the earth's total surface field anywhere on the planet \( (\approx 25 \) to \( 65 \) \( \mu \)T\( ) \), and a component cannot exceed the total.]

Given: balancing weight of mass 0.1 g \(= 0.1 \times 10^{-3}\) kg placed at one END of the needle, pole strength \(q_{m} = 20\) A m, \(g = 9.8\) m s\(^{-2}\).

Set-up. Let the needle be of length \(2l\), pivoted at its centre and free to turn in the vertical plane of the magnetic meridian. When it is held HORIZONTAL, the horizontal component \(B_{H}\) is along the needle and exerts no torque; only the VERTICAL component \(B_{V}\) does. \(B_{V}\) pulls one pole down and the other up with equal forces \(q_{m}B_{V}\), each acting at a distance \(l\) from the pivot, so it forms a couple
\(\tau_{mag} = 2 \times (q_{m}B_{V}) \times l = q_{m}B_{V}(2l) = mB_{V}\),  where \(m = q_{m}(2l)\) is the magnetic moment.

The weight is what keeps the needle horizontal, so its torque about the pivot balances that couple. The weight sits at one end, a distance \(l\) from the pivot:
\(\tau_{weight} = (Mg)\,l\), with \(Mg = 0.1 \times 10^{-3} \times 9.8 = 9.8 \times 10^{-4}\) N.

Balance.
\(q_{m}B_{V}(2l) = (Mg)\,l\)
\(B_{V} = \dfrac{Mg}{2q_{m}} = \dfrac{9.8 \times 10^{-4}}{2 \times 20} = \dfrac{9.8 \times 10^{-4}}{40}\)
\(B_{V} = 2.45 \times 10^{-5}\) T.

\(\therefore\) the vertical component of the earth's magnetic field is \(B_{V} = 2.45 \times 10^{-5}\) T \((= 0.245\) gauss\()\). Note that the length of the needle cancels, so the answer does not depend on how long the needle is.

For a paramagnetic material Curie's law gives \(\chi = C\dfrac{\mu_{0}}{T}\) (Eq. 11.21), i.e. \(\chi \propto \dfrac{1}{T}\), so \(\chi T\) is a constant. NOTE that \(T\) here is the ABSOLUTE temperature, so the Celsius values must be converted first.

Initial state: \(\chi_{1} = \chi\) at \(T_{1} = 27\,^{\circ}\)C \(= 27 + 273 = 300\) K.
Final state: \(\chi_{2} = \dfrac{\chi}{3}\) at \(T_{2} = ?\)

\(\chi_{1}T_{1} = \chi_{2}T_{2}\)
\(\chi \times 300 = \dfrac{\chi}{3} \times T_{2}\)
\(T_{2} = 3 \times 300 = 900\) K.

Converting back, \(T_{2} = 900 - 273 = 627\,^{\circ}\)C.

\(\therefore\) the susceptibility falls to \(\chi/3\) at 900 K, i.e. at \(627\,^{\circ}\)C — the susceptibility DECREASES as the temperature is raised, so the required temperature is higher than the original one, as it must be.
